misconceptions.description: Believes loop-created lambdas capture each loop value, but actually they all share the variable's final value.
Believes assigning to an outer variable inside a nested function works without nonlocal, but actually it creates a new local.
Believes closures snapshot variables at definition time, but actually they hold references to the enclosing cell.
Believes __exit__ swallows exceptions by default, but actually it only suppresses when it returns a truthy value.
Believes with is equivalent to try/finally, but actually __exit__ receives exception info and can alter control flow.
Believes the as target is always the context manager, but actually __enter__ return value can be anything.
Believes every iterable can be advanced with next(), but actually iterables like lists need iter() first.
Believes iterators can be looped over repeatedly, but actually they are exhausted after one pass.
Believes StopIteration signals a bug, but actually it is the normal end-of-iteration signal.
Believes calling a generator function executes its body, but actually it only creates a generator object.
Believes send(value) works on a fresh generator, but actually the first send must be None.
Believes close() just discards a generator, but actually it raises GeneratorExit inside it so finally blocks run.
Believes instance attributes always win, but actually data descriptors on the class take precedence.
Believes multiple inheritance resolves depth-first left-to-right, but actually Python uses C3 linearization.
Believes __getattr__ runs for every attribute access, but actually it runs only when normal lookup fails.
Believes property is a language special case, but actually it is a descriptor class like any other.
Believes non-data descriptors override instance dict entries, but actually instance attributes shadow them.
Believes a descriptor stored on an instance is invoked on access, but actually the protocol only applies to class attributes.
Believes metaclasses are needed to customize subclassing, but actually __init_subclass__ covers most cases.
Believes subclasses can pick any metaclass freely, but actually metaclass conflicts arise when bases use incompatible metaclasses.
Believes class bodies execute only when instantiated, but actually they run once at definition time.
Believes threads speed up any CPU-bound Python code, but actually the GIL serializes bytecode execution.
Believes the GIL makes compound operations atomic, but actually a read-modify-write can still interleave between bytecodes.
Believes threads are useless in Python, but actually they help I/O-bound work since the GIL is released while waiting.
Believes calling an async function starts running it, but actually it returns a coroutine that runs only when awaited or scheduled.
Believes a blocking call inside a coroutine only slows that coroutine, but actually it stalls the entire event loop.
Believes asyncio makes CPU-bound work parallel, but actually a single event loop runs one task at a time.
Believes del frees an object's memory immediately, but actually it only removes a name and the object lives while any reference remains.
Believes reference cycles always leak, but actually the cyclic garbage collector reclaims unreachable cycles.
Believes is compares values, but actually it compares object identity and small-int caching can mislead.

questions.prompt:
def make():
    x = 1
    def f():
        return x
    x = 2
    return f
print(make()())

options.text: NameError

questions.explanation: The closure f reads x through a reference to the enclosing variable, so it sees the value 2 assigned after f was defined.

questions.prompt:
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])
questions.explanation: All lambdas share the single loop variable i, which holds 2 after the loop ends, so each call returns 2.

questions.prompt:
def outer():
    count = 0
    def inc():
        count += 1
        return count
    return inc
f = outer()
f()

options.text: Returns 0 on each call
UnboundLocalError
Returns 1 after update
SyntaxError at definition

questions.explanation: Augmented assignment makes count local to inc, so reading it before assignment raises UnboundLocalError.

questions.prompt:
def outer():
    count = 0
    def inc():
        count += 1
        return count
    return inc
Which change makes inc() update the count from outer?

options.text: Add nonlocal count in inc
Make count a default arg
Use global count in inc
Replace count with a list

questions.explanation: nonlocal tells inc that count refers to the enclosing function's variable rather than creating a new local.
Every lambda reads the shared i, which is 2 after the loop, so the first lambda returns 10 plus 2.

questions.prompt:
buttons = []
for i in range(3):
    buttons.append(lambda: print(i))
Which change makes each callback print its own index?

options.text: Add nonlocal i before lambda
lambda i=i: print(i)
Reassign i = int(i) first
Wrap the loop in a list comp

questions.explanation: A default argument is evaluated at definition time, binding the current i to each lambda and avoiding the shared loop variable.

questions.prompt:
x = 'global'
def outer():
    x = 'outer'
    def inner():
        return x
    x = 'changed'
    return inner
print(outer()())

options.text: global
outer
changed
NameError

questions.explanation: inner resolves x through the enclosing function's scope, which holds 'changed' when inner is called.

questions.prompt: A class's __exit__ returns True. What happens when an exception is raised inside its with block?

options.text: The exception is suppressed but the block's remaining lines still run
The exception is suppressed regardless of what __exit__ returns
The exception is re-raised once the with block finishes
The exception is suppressed and execution continues after the with block

questions.explanation: A truthy return value from __exit__ tells the with statement to suppress the exception, so execution resumes after the block.

questions.prompt: class T: def __enter__(self): return 42 / def __exit__(self, *a): return False. After 'with T() as t: pass', what is t?

options.text: The return value of __exit__
The T instance
The T class itself
The integer 42

questions.explanation: The as target is bound to whatever __enter__ returns, here 42, not to the context manager object.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes a with statement from try/finally?

options.text: A finally clause can suppress exceptions just like __exit__ returning True
__exit__ receives the exception details and can suppress them
They are identical, so either form works in every case
__exit__ is skipped when the block raises an exception

questions.explanation: Unlike a plain finally block, __exit__ gets the exception info and its return value decides whether the exception continues.

questions.prompt: class Q: def __enter__(self): return self / def __exit__(self, t, v, tb): print('exit', t.__name__); return 0. Then 'with Q(): raise ValueError' followed by print('after'). What happens?

options.text: Prints 'exit ValueError', then ValueError propagates
Prints 'exit ValueError' and then raises TypeError
Prints 'after' with no error shown
Prints 'exit ValueError' then 'after'

questions.explanation: __exit__ returns 0, which is falsy, so the ValueError is not suppressed and propagates after __exit__ runs.

questions.prompt: def f(): with CM(): return 'x'. CM.__exit__ prints 'exit' and returns True. What does f() return?

options.text: 'x', after 'exit' prints
'x', with no exit call since nothing raised
None, because with blocks cannot return values
None, because __exit__ returned True

questions.explanation: A return inside the block triggers __exit__ before the function returns; no exception occurs, so the return value 'x' is kept.

questions.prompt: A transaction manager's __exit__ returns False. Inside its with block a KeyError is raised. What happens?

options.text: Rollback runs, then the KeyError propagates to the caller
Commit runs, then the KeyError is ignored
Rollback runs, then the error becomes a RuntimeError
The KeyError is silently suppressed after rollback

questions.explanation: Returning False from __exit__ lets the exception continue after the cleanup logic finishes.

questions.prompt: class Tag: def __init__(self,n): self.n=n / def __enter__(self): return self.n / def __exit__(self,*a): return False. What does 'with Tag('x') as n: print(n)' print?

options.text: Prints the Tag instance object
Prints x, the string returned by __enter__
Prints Tag, the class name
Prints False, the value from __exit__

questions.explanation: The as target receives __enter__'s return value, which here is the string 'x', not the Tag object.

questions.prompt: What does next(my_list) do when my_list = [1, 2, 3]?

options.text: Raises TypeError
Returns 1
Raises StopIteration
Returns [1, 2, 3]

questions.explanation: A list is an iterable, not an iterator, so it has no __next__. You must call iter() on it first to get an iterator that next() can advance.

questions.prompt: it = iter([1, 2]). What do these two lines print? print(list(it)) then print(list(it))

options.text: [1, 2] then StopIteration

questions.explanation: The first list() consumes every item, leaving the iterator exhausted. The second call finds nothing left and returns an empty list.

questions.prompt: A for loop calls next() on an iterator, which raises StopIteration. What happens?

options.text: The iterator restarts from the beginning
A warning prints and the loop continues
The error is re-raised to the caller
The loop ends quietly

questions.explanation: The for loop catches StopIteration internally as the normal end-of-iteration signal. It exits without any error being shown.

questions.prompt: def gen(): yield 1; yield 2. g = gen(). Then for x in g: pass, followed by for y in g: print(y). What prints?

options.text: Nothing, g is exhausted
A StopIteration error
1 and 2 again
1 and 2, since generators restart

questions.explanation: A generator is an iterator, so it can be consumed only once. After the first loop it is exhausted, and the second loop ends immediately without printing.

questions.prompt: it = iter(range(3)). a = sum(it), then b = sum(it). What are a and b?

options.text: a is 3 and b is 3, since range restarts
a is 3 and b is 3
a is 3 and b raises StopIteration
a is 3 and b is 0

questions.explanation: sum() consumes the iterator fully, so a is 0+1+2=3. The iterator is then exhausted, and the second sum sees no items and returns 0.

questions.prompt: class Bag has __iter__ returning iter(self.items), where items = [1, 2]. b = Bag(). Which expression gets the first item?

options.text: next(iter(b))
next(b)
next(b) after b.reset()
next(b.items)

questions.explanation: Bag is an iterable whose __iter__ builds a fresh iterator. next() needs an actual iterator, so iter(b) must be called first.

questions.prompt: def g(): return; yield. What does next(g()) do?

options.text: Raises StopIteration
Returns None to the caller
Restarts at the top of g
Raises RuntimeError, a generator bug

questions.explanation: The return statement ends the generator before any yield runs. next() then raises StopIteration, which is the normal signal that there are no more items.

questions.prompt:
def gen():
    print('start')
    yield 1

g = gen()
What is printed?

options.text: Nothing prints; gen() returns a generator.
'start' is printed, and 1 is returned.
A TypeError, since no value was sent.
'start' is printed right away.

questions.explanation: A generator function returns a generator object when called; the body runs only when next() or send() resumes it.

questions.prompt:
def g():
    x = yield 1
    print(x)

gen = g()
What happens on the first call gen.send(5)?

options.text: It runs to the first yield, then raises.
It assigns 5 to x and resumes.
It yields 5 as the first value.
TypeError: non-None send to a fresh generator.

questions.explanation: A fresh generator is suspended before its first yield, so the first send must be None; anything else raises TypeError.

questions.prompt:
def g():
    try:
        yield 1
    finally:
        print('cleanup')

gen = g()
next(gen)
gen.close()
What is printed?

options.text: Nothing, since the body already ran on call.
Nothing, since close() just discards the generator.
Nothing, since close() skips finally blocks.
cleanup

questions.explanation: close() raises GeneratorExit at the paused yield, so the finally block runs and prints cleanup.

questions.prompt:
def g():
    x = yield
    print(x)

Which code correctly prints 10 from a fresh generator gen = g()?

options.text: gen.close() then gen.send(10)
gen.send(10) then next(gen)
gen.send(10) alone
next(gen) then gen.send(10)

questions.explanation: next() advances the generator to its first yield so it can receive 10 via send; closing first ends the generator.

questions.prompt:
def g():
    try:
        yield 1
        yield 2
    finally:
        print('A')

gen = g()
next(gen)
gen.close()
What does next(gen) do now?

options.text: Prints A and yields 2.
Yields 2, since close merely pauses it.
Restarts the body and yields 1.
Raises StopIteration.

questions.explanation: After close() the generator is finished, so next() raises StopIteration without resuming the body.

options.text: As soon as lines() is called, since its body starts.
Right at the break, before the loop exits.
After the program exits, since finally waits.
When the generator is garbage-collected, calling close().

questions.explanation: The loop drops its reference to the generator, and garbage collection calls close(), which runs the finally block.

questions.prompt:
def prime(f):
    def wrapper(*a, **k):
        g = f(*a, **k)
        next(g)
        return g
    return wrapper

What does the prime decorator accomplish?

options.text: It advances the generator to its first yield so send works.
It calls close so the generator is cleaned up.
It runs the whole body to completion.
It lets send accept non-None values on a fresh generator.

questions.explanation: Calling next() once moves the generator to its first yield, which is the state send needs to accept a value.

None
fallback

questions.prompt:
class Config:
    debug = False
c = Config()
c.debug = True
print(Config.debug)

options.text: None
True
AttributeError
False

questions.explanation: Assigning c.debug creates an instance attribute and leaves the class attribute unchanged.

options.text: A
AttributeError
C

questions.explanation: C3 gives D, B, C, A, so C's x is found before A's, and __getattr__ only runs if the whole lookup fails.

options.text: AttributeError
from instance
from descriptor
the Desc object

questions.explanation: A data descriptor on the class, one defining __set__, takes precedence over a same-named entry in the instance __dict__.

options.text: Y
X
fallback

AttributeError

questions.explanation: A property is a data descriptor, so it takes precedence over a same-named entry in the instance __dict__.

dyn:greet
hi

questions.prompt: A class defines __get__ and __set__ on a descriptor attribute x. What happens on obj.x = 5?

options.text: The value 5 is stored on the class instead.
The value 5 is stored in obj.__dict__['x'] directly.
The descriptor's __set__ runs with the value 5.
The descriptor is replaced on the instance by 5.

questions.explanation: A data descriptor defines __set__, which takes priority over the instance dictionary on assignment.

questions.prompt: What is @property in Python?

options.text: A special method run once at class creation.
A descriptor class whose __get__ runs on attribute access.
A built-in keyword that bypasses attribute lookup.
A decorator that caches results in the instance dict.

questions.explanation: property is a built-in descriptor class, so its behavior comes from the same __get__ and __set__ protocol as any custom descriptor.

questions.prompt: When is __set_name__ called on a descriptor?

options.text: When the owning class is created, receiving the attribute name.
When the descriptor is stored on an instance.
The first time the attribute is set on an instance.
Each time an instance of the class is created.

questions.explanation: type creation calls __set_name__ on each class attribute that defines it, passing the owner class and attribute name.

questions.prompt:
class N:
    def __get__(self, obj, cls): return 'descriptor'
class C:
    x = N()
c = C()
c.__dict__['x'] = 1
print(c.x)

options.text: descriptor
<__main__.N object>
AttributeError

questions.explanation: N defines only __get__, so it is a non-data descriptor, and the instance dictionary entry shadows it.

questions.prompt:
class N:
    def __get__(self, obj, cls): return 'descriptor'
class C: pass
c = C()
c.y = N()
print(type(c.y).__name__)

options.text: C
descriptor
N
AttributeError

questions.explanation: The protocol applies only to class attributes, so c.y returns the stored N object and its __get__ is not called.

questions.prompt: A class defines a descriptor Ro with only __get__, assigned as class attribute val. After c = C(), what does c.val = 3 do?

options.text: Raises AttributeError because the descriptor blocks writes.
Stores 3 in the Ro object's own attribute dict.
Calls Ro.__get__ with 3 as the value.
Stores 3 in c.__dict__ under 'val'.

questions.explanation: Without __set__, Ro is a non-data descriptor, so the assignment goes into the instance dictionary.

options.text: 'Field'
None, until __set__ is called

questions.explanation: type creation calls __set_name__ on each descriptor with its attribute name, so the second Field receives 'b'.

questions.prompt: A module defines class Config whose body calls print('loaded'). Config is never instantiated. When is 'loaded' printed?

options.text: When a metaclass is attached to Config
When a Config method is first called
When the first Config instance is created
Right away, when the class statement runs

questions.explanation: The class body executes once at definition time, when the class statement runs, regardless of whether instances exist.

questions.prompt: Without a metaclass, how can a base class run code each time a subclass is defined?

options.text: Define __init_subclass__ on the base class
Define __new__ on a metaclass
Override __call__ on the base class
Pass metaclass= in the subclass header

questions.explanation: __init_subclass__ is called on the base whenever a subclass is created, giving a lighter alternative to a metaclass.

questions.prompt: class Counter: print('defining') is followed by c1 = Counter() and c2 = Counter(). How many times is 'defining' printed?

options.text: Zero times until an instance exists
Once, when the class statement runs
Twice, once for each Counter() call
Once, after any metaclass __init__ runs

questions.explanation: The class body runs once at definition; instantiating the class does not re-execute it.

questions.prompt:
class M1(type): pass
class M2(type): pass
class A(metaclass=M1): pass
class B(metaclass=M2): pass
class C(A, B): pass
What happens when C is defined?

options.text: C gets a merged metaclass of M1 and M2
TypeError: M1 and M2 are unrelated
C uses M2, since B is the last base
C uses M1, since A is the first base

questions.explanation: Python picks the most derived metaclass among the bases; if neither metaclass derives from the other, the class statement raises a metaclass conflict TypeError.

questions.prompt: You want every subclass of Plugin added to a registry when it is defined. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Define __init_subclass__ on Plugin that adds cls to a registry
Give Plugin a metaclass whose __new__ registers each class
Call registry.add in Plugin's class body once
Override Plugin.__init__ to register type(self)

questions.explanation: __init_subclass__ runs for each new subclass at its definition, which handles this without a metaclass; __init__ runs per instance, not per subclass.

options.text: C, A, B
A, C, B
C, B, A
A, B, C

questions.explanation: The class body runs first to fill the namespace, then Meta.__new__ runs, then Meta.__init__ runs on the created class.

questions.prompt:
class Abc1(type): pass
class Abc2(Abc1): pass
class Base(metaclass=Abc1): pass
class Child(Base, metaclass=Abc2): pass
What is type(Child)?

options.text: type, because an explicit metaclass resets it
Abc2, a subclass of Abc1
TypeError, since Child cannot change Base's metaclass
Abc1, inherited from Base

questions.explanation: A subclass may name a metaclass that derives from the metaclasses of its bases, so Abc2 is chosen; the conflict only arises when the metaclasses are unrelated.

questions.prompt: Two threads each run a CPU-bound pure-Python loop on CPython. Compared with running them one after another, what is the most likely result?

options.text: About the same time, since the GIL keeps each counter update atomic
About the same total time, since the GIL lets one thread run bytecode at a time
Much less time, since the GIL is released during arithmetic
Roughly half the total time, since both threads run in parallel

questions.explanation: The GIL serializes execution of Python bytecode, so CPU-bound threads gain no parallel speedup in CPython.

questions.prompt: What does the GIL primarily protect in CPython?

options.text: Internal interpreter state such as object reference counts
Network sockets during blocking reads
Thread creation overhead, so threads start faster
Shared user variables from interleaving at any point in the code

questions.explanation: The GIL protects CPython's internal structures, like reference counts, from concurrent corruption, not the user's program-level logic.

questions.prompt: Ten threads each download a different URL with blocking requests calls. Why can this finish much faster than one thread doing them in turn?

options.text: The GIL is released while each thread waits on the network
The GIL makes the shared response buffer updates atomic
Each thread runs on its own core without needing the GIL
Threads cannot speed this up, since the GIL blocks all of them

questions.explanation: Blocking I/O calls release the GIL, so while one thread waits, others can run Python code and issue their own requests.

questions.prompt: A pure-Python image filter loop over millions of pixels is CPU-bound. Which change most likely gives a real speedup on CPython?

options.text: Raise the thread switch interval to ten seconds
Wrap the whole loop in a threading.Lock
Split the pixel work across processes with multiprocessing
Use more threads, since each thread gets its own GIL

questions.explanation: Separate processes each have their own interpreter and GIL, so CPU-bound work can run truly in parallel across cores.

questions.prompt: Two threads each run counter += 1 on a shared int 100000 times with no lock. What is the likely final value?

options.text: Exactly 200000, since the GIL makes each += atomic
Exactly 100000, since one thread's writes overwrite the other's
Exactly 200000, since the threads run the loops in parallel without interference
Possibly below 200000, since increments can interleave

questions.explanation: The += reads, adds, and writes in separate bytecodes, so a thread switch between them can lose updates even under the GIL.

questions.prompt: A service uses a thread pool for 500 slow REST API calls and also runs a pure-Python checksum loop over large files. Which split is best?

options.text: Threads for the API calls, processes for the checksum loop
Threads for both, since the GIL is released during the checksum loop
Threads for both, since the GIL protects the shared checksum state
Processes for both, since threads cannot overlap network waits

questions.explanation: Network waits release the GIL so threads help there, while the pure-Python CPU loop needs processes to use multiple cores.

questions.prompt: Many threads run d[k] = d.get(k, 0) + 1 on one shared dict. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Safe, since get and set each run as one bytecode
Safe on multicore, since the GIL does not apply there
Safe under the GIL, since dict operations are atomic
A lock is still needed, since get and set can interleave

questions.explanation: The read and write are separate steps, so another thread can switch in between and cause a lost update despite the GIL.

questions.prompt: What does calling `fetch()` return when `fetch` is defined as `async def` and called without await?

options.text: The fetched result, computed immediately
A coroutine object whose body has not started
A finished Task already running in the background
The result after its body blocks the thread

questions.explanation: Calling an async function only creates a coroutine object. Its body runs when it is awaited or wrapped in a task and scheduled on the loop.

questions.prompt: Two tasks run under asyncio. One calls time.sleep(2) inside a coroutine. What happens to a third ready task meanwhile?

options.text: It runs on another thread automatically
It runs normally, since the loop preempts sleeping tasks
It runs normally, since just one coroutine is delayed
It waits, because the loop thread is blocked

questions.explanation: time.sleep blocks the single thread running the event loop, so no other task can run until it returns. Use await asyncio.sleep to yield control instead.

questions.prompt: What does `await other_coro()` do inside a coroutine?

options.text: Suspends this coroutine so the loop can run other tasks
Runs the awaited call on a separate CPU core
Schedules the call and continues without waiting
Starts the awaited call in a new thread

questions.explanation: Await hands control back to the event loop until the awaited coroutine finishes. The loop uses that time to run other ready tasks on the same thread.

questions.prompt: Four coroutines each run a pure-Python loop of 10 million iterations with no awaits, all in one event loop. What total speedup over running them sequentially is realistic?

options.text: About 4x, since each task gets its own core
About 1x, since one task runs at a time
About 2x, since the loop runs two tasks at once
About 4x, since awaiting each coroutine starts it early

questions.explanation: A single event loop runs one task at a time on one thread, and these tasks never yield. CPU-bound work gains no parallel speedup from asyncio.

questions.prompt: Code calls `x = job()` on an `async def job()` and does nothing else. What happens?

options.text: The body runs in the background until it finishes
The body runs once synchronously before returning
The main thread blocks until the body completes
Nothing runs, and Python warns the coroutine was never awaited

questions.explanation: Calling an async function returns an unstarted coroutine object. Without await or scheduling, its body never executes and Python emits a warning.

questions.prompt: An async web handler calls json.loads on a 200 MB payload synchronously. Other requests on the same server slow down. Why?

options.text: asyncio moves the parse to a separate thread, so the server should not stall
The synchronous parse blocks the loop, so no other coroutine runs
The parse slows just this handler, and others keep running
Calling the async handler ran the parse before the loop started

questions.explanation: The parse is a blocking call on the single event loop thread. While it runs, the loop cannot switch to other requests, so all of them stall.

questions.prompt: Eight CPU-bound image resizes run as tasks in one asyncio loop. Which change best uses all cores?

options.text: Add more tasks so the loop spreads the work
Call each resize without await to start it now
Gather the eight coroutines to run in parallel
Offload each resize to a process pool with run_in_executor

questions.explanation: Processes run in parallel on separate cores, and run_in_executor hands the CPU work off without blocking the loop. Gathering or adding tasks still runs them one at a time on one thread.

questions.prompt: x = [1]; y = x; del x. Is the list still alive?

options.text: No, del frees the list immediately
Yes, y still references it
Yes, but y holds a separate copy
No, the list was moved over to y

questions.explanation: del only removes the name x. The list stays alive because y still refers to it, so it is freed only when no references remain.

questions.prompt: p = [1]; q = [1]; print(p is q)

options.text: True, equal contents means same object
True, both lists hold 1
True, p was freed when q was made
False, they are two separate list objects

questions.explanation: is compares identity, and each list literal creates a new object. Equal contents do not make two objects identical.

questions.prompt: a = []; a.append(a); del a. Is the list reclaimed without manual help?

options.text: Yes, because del frees the list at once
No, the self-reference keeps it alive forever
